title: What Happened to HackerOne?
excerpt: The rise and fall of the largest bug bounty platform in the world
content_html:
So…what’s going on at HackerOne lately? It might be time for a wellness check.

If you are new to the bug bounty space (1-3 years), you might not have any idea what I’m talking about.

But as a properly washed-up bug bounty hunter who lived through the golden era of HackerOne, I think it’s time to address the elephant in the room.

For some context, I started as a hacker on HackerOne in 2017. When I began working in tech, that hands-on experience was extremely useful for managing a bug bounty program, since I knew what researchers wanted, and how to interact with them.

As a result, I have managed multiple large bug bounty programs on HackerOne across various companies from 2018 to 2025 and I’ve been on both sides of the equation.

What I’m about to talk about comes from first-hand experience, both as a researcher and as a bug bounty program manager, and many, many years of direct conversations with HackerOne, both publicly and privately.

Background #

To start, I think it’s important to realize what HackerOne was originally designed to be.

In 2011, two ethical hackers, Jobert Abma and Michiel Prins, set out to find security vulnerabilities in 100 of the largest tech companies. They succeeded and found bugs in Google, Facebook, Apple, Microsoft, Twitter, and many others. At this point in time, the landscape for ethical security research was risky, legally dubious, and very scary for security researchers.

Not only was there significant personal liability, but there had been multiple instances of hackers being criminally charged and sentenced to jail time for finding and reporting security vulnerabilities prior to this. Much of this was due to specific arbitrary lines drawn in the sand which, if crossed, made you a bad actor, but if not crossed, made you a potentially bad actor but technically not one.

Bug Bounty Platforms like HackerOne were designed to directly address this issue. It created a safe mutual space for companies and hackers to connect, and it paved the way for ethical hackers to submit security vulnerabilities to companies, with full consent, and get paid for that work. This was a huge milestone. You no longer had to worry about getting dragged to court (or jail) for finding an IDOR that leaked customer data. Instead, you got a “thank you” and a cash payout for making everyone a little safer.

This operating model was the foundation for bug bounty and remained that way for the next 5+ years.

The Golden Age of HackerOne and Live Hacking Events #

During this period, there was a very strong and explicit focus for the business: how do we make this the best possible product for hackers?

The people running the business day-to-day were hackers, hacker-adjacent, and most (if not all) were face-to-face with hackers on a regular basis.

From 2017 to 2020, HackerOne was doing Live Hacking Events (LHEs) every few months. These were exclusive events where the top bug bounty researchers around the world would fly into a location, be given a target, and go absolutely ham finding critical vulnerabilities. LHEs were a huge value prop for programs. During a 1-3 day period, you would get more high and critical security reports than you would have received for the whole year otherwise.

Every event had a 1-of-1 custom designed poster with graphics, hacker usernames, stickers and challenge coins. It’s hard to overstate what an incredible and productive period this was for HackerOne and their top programs.

These events were exclusive and highly coveted; invites and +1s were practically their own currency. And the environment at these events was surreal. You would be given free flights and hotels around the world, and spend a few days surrounded by the best and most skilled bug bounty hunters in the world. These researchers would regularly find some of the most impactful bugs using their own novel techniques, and all while sharing tips and tricks in one-off conversations that could not be replicated anywhere else.

Prior to the advent of live hacking events, most security researcher circles were small, isolated, and sharing information publicly was practically unheard of. LHEs created a way for security researchers to connect with each other, and essentially created a whole new community within infosec. Most of my closest friends nowadays are people who I met through the live hacking scene, and I am extremely grateful to HackerOne for that.

LHEs were not the only area where HackerOne was building and establish a community for security researchers. They created a HackerOne Community space to organize meetups, online events, workshops, and CTFs. They created regional clubs, and appointed hackers who lived there as ambassadors to help foster and grow local researcher communities all around the world.

But slowly but surely, things began to change. The community groups and events lost momentum and fizzled out. The custom designed silkscreen LHE posters became cheap low-effort laser prints. The people who had dedicated years to creating and running incredible events were laid off or left. The LHE invitation and scoring systems became (even more) exclusive, gamified, and exceedingly calculated.

So one by one, the dominoes began to fall.

The Profit Problem #

Before going further, I think it’s important to get into the “why” behind these changes that started happening. Sometime around 2020 or 2021, HackerOne was forced to come face-to-face with a very important question that every business must ask itself at some point: “How do we make money?”

To understand how HackerOne even was able to survive as a business, you have to first know that HackerOne was basically running entirely on VC money for the first 10 years of its existence. Between 2014 and 2022, the company did a seed round almost every 2 years, raising a total of $160M. If a company is self-sustaining, there is little-to-no reason to continue raising money unless you have an incredibly high burn-rate, which would be odd for a company with such little infrastructure and technical innovation.

If you know anything about VC, you know how this tends to work; they give you money, and in return, you give them indirect control of the business through board seats, advisory positions, and other leverage mechanisms. The VCs gave the money, so the VCs get the power.

Rome did not fall in a day, and neither did HackerOne. The paradigm shift started slowly, and then all at once. The core technology driving the platform began to stagnate. Very little changed within the platform. The UI remained tired and “functional”. The performance remained lacking.

But the VCs looked at their playbook and realized that the easiest way to make money was simple: get more customers.

First, the founding CEO was replaced with a corporate CEO. Instead of a 20% cut of bounties paid, they shifted to capacity-based fee structures, annual contracts, and locking customers into multi-year deals.

And then, sales. SALES SALES SALES!! They were fully convinced that sales were the bread and butter of the business. So instead of basing the company around hackers, they leaned into sales.

More customers = more annual contracts = more predictable long-term revenue. Once a customer is locked in, they are fed stats and numbers and greased up to keep them happy, but also to keep demands low. When contract renewal comes up, they are given massive (30-60%) discounts in exchange for a multi-year contract in order to keep them locked in and paying.

Account Managers would have regular meetings with customers and encourage them to raise bounties to stay competitive and attractive to hackers. They would tell you, “Hackers want to spend time focused on the highest-paying programs”.

HackerOne was proud of this and encouraged the behavior internally. They gave out rewards, free vacations, and encouraged their rapidly growing sales team to sign new customers as much as possible.

As this continued, things continued to degrade for everyone involved.

For triagers, the best ones (who were hackers themselves) burned out and quit. The pay was too low and the workload was too much.

For hackers, the triage experience declined, and they became flooded with excessive amounts of low-quality programs.

For customers, the quality of reports went down, the costs went up, and the race to the bottom began.

And for everyone, the platform experience declined and never evolved.

Typically at this point, market economics would dictate that this is where a competitor takes your business and you must improve to retain market share. But bug bounty is an oligopoly, and there are 3 companies that control almost the entire market.

So instead, HackerOne was forced to create a new exclusive opportunity called the “Hacker Success Program” (HSP). This is a dedicated space for top hackers to get direct support from HackerOne for anything bug bounty related. They were assigned to a Hacker Success Manager (HSM) who was employed by HackerOne, and they could leverage that relationship to navigate miscommunications, bad program experiences, low or inaccurate bounty payouts, and much more. They also use this space to offer unique opportunities like H1 challenges for hackers in the HSP group.

One thing I want to call out is that while this is a great idea in theory, in practice it created a completely lopsided playing field for new hackers. You have basically zero ways to advocate or work through problems (good luck working with HackerOne support), so the rich get richer and you are given the option to deal with it or get lost unless/until you are a top hacker. Oddly enough, it would be much easier to become a top hacker if you had access to these resources in the first place.

Anyway, for some hackers, the HSP revolutionized what was previously an impossible brick wall. If you got screwed over by a company who failed to understand the security impact of your report, you could now lean on your HSM to help get a direct line of communication to the company and try to resolve that.

But for others, the HSP highlighted one of the core underlying failures that has plagued HackerOne for years: stagnating feature development. Even if you are part of the exclusive HSP group, you still don’t have the ability to do one important thing, which is to invoke change and development within the platform.

And yet, for some reason, HackerOne decided to take a performative approach to this, going as far as to create a dedicated platform feedback channel, but doing absolutely nothing with any of that feedback. I cannot even count how many pieces of individual feedback and suggestions have been posted in there, with positively zero action from HackerOne.

The AI Era #

And then, around 2021, we all entered a new period of human history: the rise of AI and LLMs.

Beginning around this time, we all began to witness the huge gains in velocity and the capabilities of LLMs. You could now one-shot features in a fraction of the time, build custom tools, and overall get more done in less time.

But this is where HackerOne took a confusing turn. It is truly baffling to me how HackerOne managed to fumble this technology in the worst way possible. They had a 10-year backlog of feature requests, and were handed one of the most powerful software development tools in the last 50 years. But instead of using this to improve the platform and add long-requested features, they decided to move toward creating “their own” AI assistant called Hai. Not only was Hai just a wrapper on top of OpenAI, but it barely had any real unique capabilities to help hackers or programs do what they had been requesting from HackerOne to add to the core platform.

On top of this, the driving force behind the company, the hackers and co-founders who started the business, were quietly shoved away into the dungeon of HackerOne. The website has them listed as part of the executive team, but they are puppets in their own business, barely getting to work on the product they built from the ground up.

The Enshittification of HackerOne #

For almost 10 years, Marten Mickos served as CEO of HackerOne. Some hackers loved Marten; others had mixed feelings. Personally, my interactions with him were somewhere between fine and good. But I do believe that he was very passionate about bug bounty and did a lot of good for the company during his time as CEO.

But in late 2024, Marten was replaced by Kara Sprague, the former Chief Product Officer at F5. You might be asking yourself, what does a CPO of a networking company know about hacking and bug bounty?

Honestly, I am not sure. What I will say is that there are mixed signals online regarding what happened to BIG-IP during her time as CPO at F5.

But that didn’t stop the board from deciding she was the right fit for the future of the company. And this was neither the first nor the last in a series of questionable business decisions made by HackerOne.

As AI agents continued to grow and shift into various identities, HackerOne’s identity also began to shift. Slowly but steadily, HackerOne rebranded itself around a newly invented industry category: “CTEM”, or “Continuous Threat Exposure Management”.

HackerOne quickly began to evolve into a soulless corporation obsessed with numbers, business objectives, and B2B sales. They switched from talking about bug bounty programs, live hacking events, and how they could help you stay secure, to promoting their in-house AI security product and continuous security monitoring tool.

Wait, what? What in-house AI security product?

Your Reports Are Yours, We Promise #

Sometimes, it all starts with a tweet.

In February 2026, well-known hacker zseano noticed that there was a surge in HackerOne employees leaving the company and asked why that would be happening.

This ended up revealing that HackerOne had made ToS updates which made it so that reports submitted on HackerOne could be used to train AI models.

As you might expect, this created quite a bit of noise, especially within the HSP chats. One thing I’ve noticed is that the modern day HackerOne only ever lets the founders out of the dungeon for damage control, and this was a perfect time to pull that lever.

Within 24 hours, Alex Rice, co-founder, CTO (and CISO…?) of HackerOne emerged from the dungeon to perform damage control. (This was the first time he had ever messaged in the HSP general chat since it was created two years earlier).

We do not train, fine-tune, or otherwise improve GenAI or large language models on researcher data. That includes Agentic PTaaS.

https://docs.hackerone.com/en/articles/10908081-hai-security-trust

And when asked to remove Section 3.1 of the ToS, Alex promised that this would be taken care of and made clearer in an upcoming update to the ToS.

Within a week, CEO Kara Sprague had been looped in and made a fluffy LinkedIn post explaining that

HackerOne does not train generative AI models, internally or through third-party providers, on researcher submissions or customer confidential data.

Researcher submissions are not used to train, fine-tune, or otherwise improve generative AI models. This applies across our platform, including capabilities used within our Agentic PTaaS offering and our in-platform AI, Hai.

Alex Rice even went on to the Critical Thinking Bug Bounty Podcast and did a guest spot to talk about this issue specifically and shut down any concerns about report data being used to train AI models.

Amazing, that’s settled then. HackerOne doesn’t use researcher data to train AI models.

…Right?

Just Kidding They Never Were #

Unfortunately for us, the present-day HackerOne follows a rather impressive PR damage control playbook:

  1. Address fears
  2. Ease concerns
  3. Don’t change anything

About two months after this drama, someone mentioned in the HSP chat that they had noticed a comment from hackerone-agent on one of their reports and wanted to know if this was an AI agent or an actual human.

The response from one of the HackerOne product managers was:

This is a preliminary review done by AI […] The H1 triage process has a step called “H1 Intake” […] which we’ve automated for certain reports to make sure they reach the “Validation team” faster.

And when asked whether “certain reports” meant certain report types or whether a program could enable it everywhere, they responded:

We’re running the analysis on all reports, the AI determines what can be sent directly to the validation team vs what needs to be reviewed by a human from the intake team first. […] The system also learns from behaviour so, if a recommendation is rejected […] it will take these into account with its recommendations as well.

Hang on a second.

I thought that researcher submissions are not used to train, fine-tune, or otherwise improve generative AI models.

But now all reports are being run through an AI system, and the system is using the outcomes of those reports to influence how it handles future reports. So is that technically “fine-tuning”? Technically, no.

So how can both of these things be possible?

Well, when I asked this, I received an incredible copy-paste response of what Alex Rice had said back in February:

Hai does not train, fine-tune, or otherwise improve GenAI or large language models on customer or researcher data: https://docs.hackerone.com/en/articles/10908081-hai-security-trust

They then followed up with an explanation that appeared to contradict this:

Storing learnings in our DB is something different than training/fine-tuning a model on how to behave. We store the rejection reasons in our DB to cross reference and augment the reasoning the agent does when determining next steps. […] The agent will pick this up from behaviour the customer has done on past reports and use that to memorize and augment the reasoning for new reports.

So yes, HackerOne is not building model weights from your report data or “training” on it in the traditional sense.

But that is a distinction without any meaningful difference to the researchers whose data is being used. The system is still learning from report data in the practical sense that matters: past reports change future automated behavior.

Call it memory, retrieval, contextual learning, or whatever you want. For the purpose of deciding whether researcher data is being used to improve the system, the distinction is functionally equivalent.

And as a cherry on top, a few days later, HackerOne published a blog post stating:

As AI-assisted submissions have grown, we’ve invested heavily in AI-powered triage and validation on our own platform. Our agentic AI system, Hai, now handles initial classification, deduplication, and validation of incoming reports, working alongside our human security analysts.

The Boiling Point #

By this point, I had lost all faith in HackerOne. I’d been around for so many years and through so many seasons that there was really no point in leaving anything off the table.

So I posted a long message in the HSP chat, echoing many of the things I’ve said in this blog.

What happened as a result was actually really surprising: many other top hackers in the HSP agreed, echoed the same concerns, and called for change.

I figured, surely HackerOne will have to respond to this.

And they did.

Co-founder Michiel Prins was allowed to leave the HackerOne dungeon to perform damage control with this absolute banger of an AI slop response:

You’re right to call this out. Parts of the platform and overall experience have not moved fast enough, and that’s frustrating.

We have been prioritizing work that improves outcomes for both customers and researchers. Triage is a clear example. Speed and consistency there have improved materially, and that matters for everyone on the platform. Report Assistant may not be targeted at the caliber hacker in this channel, but it has been a significant enhancement for the largest part of the community - hackers earlier in their career - and this has led to much clearer reports for triage to analyze and accelerate overall throughput.

At the same time, there is a bigger shift happening with AI. There is a lot of noise about AI replacing security researchers. We do not believe that. We are investing to make sure researchers become more important, not less. A lot of that work is happening on the customer side of the marketplace.

That said, the gap you are pointing to on day-to-day usability and acting on feedback is real. We need to do a better job there, and we need to show that progress more clearly.

And then, per the playbook, they waited for the community to move on, brushed it under the rug, and nothing changed.

We Must Calm the Masses #

Well that was true until June, when rez0 (co-host of the Critical Thinking Bug Bounty Podcast) asked about the new “HackerOne Continuous Testing” product that had just launched:

The page (before it was updated) very clearly stated:

Testing is sharpened using context from HackerOne’s 12+ years of real-world vulnerability data and your prior H1 Bounty findings, so agents know where to focus

HackerOne immediately tried to run this back and claim that this was actually not true. I find it hard to understand how a company can be so incredibly disconnected from its own values, but only when it’s brought up by hackers who look closely and ask questions.

All the behavior over the last few months embodies “oops we didn’t mean to say the quiet part out loud”, and certainly not “we don’t do that”.

And honestly at this point if you have to do this much damage control, you might as well just own it.

I won’t even begin to break these statements down because there’s so much word soup that it’s mind-numbing.

As I write this post, I am exhausted from trying to perform the mental gymnastics required to believe all this.

Actions speak louder than words, and it’s pretty clear at this point what’s going on.

Feel free to skip ahead, but in an effort to be fair I’ll provide the replies from not one but two HackerOne co-founders (wow a double dungeon release):

No change in direction. There is zero training on researcher data.

This language isn’t even talking about vulnerability discovery. What happens when you point a “recon agent” at an attack surface?

Noise.

That’s the context being talked about here – Scope. Out of scope. Informative. Ineligible findings. This same contextual feedback loop is available to researchers (and, increasingly, their agents) through our intake agents & full triage process.

We continue to need to do much better on accompanying simplified marketing language with technical architecture documentation, and we need to do a better job at reinforcing the defense in depth narrative – there are no silver bullets here. Nowhere in our vision is a 100% AI human-free future.

- Alex Rice

and

Sorry for the confusion this paragraph has caused. It was meant to capture how our recon agents find out where to focus and where not to focus based on prior results in a customer’s program (mapping the attack surface), not find new vulnerabilities based on researcher submissions. We have adjusted the paragraph in the H1 Continuous Testing page and buttoned up our documentation. H1 Continuous Testing is based on the same approach and methodologies as the H1 Agentic Pentest offering announced in January. Here is the documentation on how those agentic products reason & use context for security testing workflows.

But let’s focus on the underlying concern: is H1 using researcher submissions to then deploy agents and find that vulnerability using their techniques in other customers? No.

That is a model that can be a win-win-win for everyone in the long run, but we don’t yet have the foundations in place to provide proper recognition and rewards for researchers in such a model. We’re envisioning a platform where researchers drive the frontier, agents provide the scale, and researchers get proper recognition for their impact. Imagine this: you discover a novel technique to find a vulnerability. We operationalize it across every customer’s attack surface that shows signs of exposure. Customers get protected. You get compensated not just for one report, but proportionally to the impact you generate across the platform. That is fundamentally a better deal for researchers than the current one-bounty-per-report model. And it is also a win for customers as it narrows the exposure window.

But the reality is that it’s just a vision right now. We are not there yet. This requires careful work across product, policy and researcher engagement models to build it right. Right now, we are still focused on building foundational agentic capabilities for testing, accelerating validation and triage, prioritization, and remediation. These have to work reliably first before we can layer on a researcher-driven attack library and incentive model that does justice to the contribution. We also owe it to customers not to just dump findings on them without the tooling to act on them.

The long term is about partnership, not replacement. We want to build incentive structures that support this vision. It’s unexplored territory, and we want to get it right with you.

- Michiel Prins

along with a HackerOne official™ tweet to calm the masses:

Conclusion #

Today as I look at HackerOne, it’s hard to even recognize the company that was started back in 2012. The values have shifted, the soul has been gutted, and the core identity has been lost. A sad ending for our hero’s journey.

So, where do we go from here?

Well, I have some final thoughts for each party involved in this twisting tale.

To HackerOne: It was nice knowing you. All I can hope is that you can find your true identity again one day. Although I doubt that will ever happen.

To the founders: I hope you got paid well, that you can exit, and that you go do something cool again.

To the hackers: Know your worth. Bug bounty platforms cannot exist without hackers.

To the companies: You don’t need HackerOne anymore. The tokens to build your own in-house platform cost less than single year of HackerOne.

And to whoever is fired up: The market is ready for a disruption. The tools are in your hands. Build what HackerOne could have been.

Godspeed and thanks for reading if you made it this far.

If you got screwed over by a company who failed to understand the security impact of your report, you could now lean on your HSM to help get a direct line of communication to the company and try to resolve that. But for others, the HSP highlighted one of the core underlying failures that has plagued HackerOne for years: stagnating feature development. Even if you are part of the exclusive HSP group, you still don’t have the ability to do one important thing, which is to invoke change and development within the platform. And yet, for some reason, HackerOne decided to take a performative approach to this, going as far as to create a dedicated platform feedback channel, but doing absolutely nothing with any of that feedback. I cannot even count how many pieces of individual feedback and suggestions have been posted in there, with positively zero action from HackerOne. The AI Era # And then, around 2021, we all entered a new period of human history: the rise of AI and LLMs. Beginning around this time, we all began to witness the huge gains in velocity and the capabilities of LLMs. You could now one-shot features in a fraction of the time, build custom tools, and overall get more done in less time. But this is where HackerOne took a confusing turn. It is truly baffling to me how HackerOne managed to fumble this technology in the worst way possible. They had a 10-year backlog of feature requests, and were handed one of the most powerful software development tools in the last 50 years. But instead of using this to improve the platform and add long-requested features, they decided to move toward creating “their own” AI assistant called Hai. Not only was Hai just a wrapper on top of OpenAI, but it barely had any real unique capabilities to help hackers or programs do what they had been requesting from HackerOne to add to the core platform. On top of this, the driving force behind the company, the hackers and co-founders who started the business, were quietly shoved away into the dungeon of HackerOne. The website has them listed as part of the executive team, but they are puppets in their own business, barely getting to work on the product they built from the ground up. The Enshittification of HackerOne # For almost 10 years, Marten Mickos served as CEO of HackerOne. Some hackers loved Marten; others had mixed feelings. Personally, my interactions with him were somewhere between fine and good. But I do believe that he was very passionate about bug bounty and did a lot of good for the company during his time as CEO. But in late 2024, Marten was replaced by Kara Sprague, the former Chief Product Officer at F5. You might be asking yourself, what does a CPO of a networking company know about hacking and bug bounty? Honestly, I am not sure. What I will say is that there are mixed signals online regarding what happened to BIG-IP during her time as CPO at F5. But that didn’t stop the board from deciding she was the right fit for the future of the company. And this was neither the first nor the last in a series of questionable business decisions made by HackerOne. As AI agents continued to grow and shift into various identities, HackerOne’s identity also began to shift. Slowly but steadily, HackerOne rebranded itself around a newly invented industry category: “CTEM”, or “Continuous Threat Exposure Management”. HackerOne quickly began to evolve into a soulless corporation obsessed with numbers, business objectives, and B2B sales. They switched from talking about bug bounty programs, live hacking events, and how they could help you stay secure, to promoting their in-house AI security product and continuous security monitoring tool. Wait, what? What in-house AI security product? Your Reports Are Yours, We Promise # Sometimes, it all starts with a tweet. In February 2026, well-known hacker zseano noticed that there was a surge in HackerOne employees leaving the company and asked why that would be happening. This ended up revealing that HackerOne had made ToS updates which made it so that reports submitted on HackerOne could be used to train AI models. As you might expect, this created quite a bit of noise, especially within the HSP chats. One thing I’ve noticed is that the modern day HackerOne only ever lets the founders out of the dungeon for damage control, and this was a perfect time to pull that lever. Within 24 hours, Alex Rice, co-founder, CTO (and CISO…?) of HackerOne emerged from the dungeon to perform damage control. (This was the first time he had ever messaged in the HSP general chat since it was created two years earlier). We do not train, fine-tune, or otherwise improve GenAI or large language models on researcher data. That includes Agentic PTaaS. https://docs.hackerone.com/en/articles/10908081-hai-security-trust And when asked to remove Section 3.1 of the ToS, Alex promised that this would be taken care of and made clearer in an upcoming update to the ToS. Within a week, CEO Kara Sprague had been looped in and made a fluffy LinkedIn post explaining that HackerOne does not train generative AI models, internally or through third-party providers, on researcher submissions or customer confidential data. Researcher submissions are not used to train, fine-tune, or otherwise improve generative AI models. This applies across our platform, including capabilities used within our Agentic PTaaS offering and our in-platform AI, Hai. Alex Rice even went on to the Critical Thinking Bug Bounty Podcast and did a guest spot to talk about this issue specifically and shut down any concerns about report data being used to train AI models. Amazing, that’s settled then. HackerOne doesn’t use researcher data to train AI models. …Right? Just Kidding They Never Were # Unfortunately for us, the present-day HackerOne follows a rather impressive PR damage control playbook: Address fears Ease concerns Don’t change anything About two months after this drama, someone mentioned in the HSP chat that they had noticed a comment from hackerone-agent on one of their reports and wanted to know if this was an AI agent or an actual human. The response from one of the HackerOne product managers was: This is a preliminary review done by AI […] The H1 triage process has a step called “H1 Intake” […] which we’ve automated for certain reports to make sure they reach the “Validation team” faster. And when asked whether “certain reports” meant certain report types or whether a program could enable it everywhere, they responded: We’re running the analysis on all reports, the AI determines what can be sent directly to the validation team vs what needs to be reviewed by a human from the intake team first. […] The system also learns from behaviour so, if a recommendation is rejected […] it will take these into account with its recommendations as well. Hang on a second. I thought that researcher submissions are not used to train, fine-tune, or otherwise improve generative AI models. But now all reports are being run through an AI system, and the system is using the outcomes of those reports to influence how it handles future reports. So is that technically “fine-tuning”? Technically, no. So how can both of these things be possible? Well, when I asked this, I received an incredible copy-paste response of what Alex Rice had said back in February: Hai does not train, fine-tune, or otherwise improve GenAI or large language models on customer or researcher data: https://docs.hackerone.com/en/articles/10908081-hai-security-trust They then followed up with an explanation that appeared to contradict this: Storing learnings in our DB is something different than training/fine-tuning a model on how to behave. We store the rejection reasons in our DB to cross reference and augment the reasoning the agent does when determining next steps. […] The agent will pick this up from behaviour the customer has done on past reports and use that to memorize and augment the reasoning for new reports. So yes, HackerOne is not building model weights from your report data or “training” on it in the traditional sense. But that is a distinction without any meaningful difference to the researchers whose data is being used. The system is still learning from report data in the practical sense that matters: past reports change future automated behavior. Call it memory, retrieval, contextual learning, or whatever you want. For the purpose of deciding whether researcher data is being used to improve the system, the distinction is functionally equivalent. And as a cherry on top, a few days later, HackerOne published a blog post stating: As AI-assisted submissions have grown, we’ve invested heavily in AI-powered triage and validation on our own platform. Our agentic AI system, Hai, now handles initial classification, deduplication, and validation of incoming reports, working alongside our human security analysts. The Boiling Point # By this point, I had lost all faith in HackerOne. I’d been around for so many years and through so many seasons that there was really no point in leaving anything off the table. So I posted a long message in the HSP chat, echoing many of the things I’ve said in this blog. What happened as a result was actually really surprising: many other top hackers in the HSP agreed, echoed the same concerns, and called for change. I figured, surely HackerOne will have to respond to this. And they did. Co-founder Michiel Prins was allowed to leave the HackerOne dungeon to perform damage control with this absolute banger of an AI slop response: You’re right to call this out. Parts of the platform and overall experience have not moved fast enough, and that’s frustrating. We have been prioritizing work that improves outcomes for both customers and researchers. Triage is a clear example. Speed and consistency there have improved materially, and that matters for everyone on the platform. Report Assistant may not be targeted at the caliber hacker in this channel, but it has been a significant enhancement for the largest part of the community - hackers earlier in their career - and this has led to much clearer reports for triage to analyze and accelerate overall throughput. At the same time, there is a bigger shift happening with AI. There is a lot of noise about AI replacing security researchers. We do not believe that. We are investing to make sure researchers become more important, not less. A lot of that work is happening on the customer side of the marketplace. That said, the gap you are pointing to on day-to-day usability and acting on feedback is real. We need to do a better job there, and we need to show that progress more clearly. And then, per the playbook, they waited for the community to move on, brushed it under the rug, and nothing changed. We Must Calm the Masses # Well that was true until June, when rez0 (co-host of the Critical Thinking Bug Bounty Podcast) asked about the new “HackerOne Continuous Testing” product that had just launched: The page (before it was updated) very clearly stated: Testing is sharpened using context from HackerOne’s 12+ years of real-world vulnerability data and your prior H1 Bounty findings, so agents know where to focus HackerOne immediately tried to run this back and claim that this was actually not true. I find it hard to understand how a company can be so incredibly disconnected from its own values, but only when it’s brought up by hackers who look closely and ask questions. All the behavior over the last few months embodies “oops we didn’t mean to say the quiet part out loud”, and certainly not “we don’t do that”. And honestly at this point if you have to do this much damage control, you might as well just own it. I won’t even begin to break these statements down because there’s so much word soup that it’s mind-numbing. As I write this post, I am exhausted from trying to perform the mental gymnastics required to believe all this. Actions speak louder than words, and it’s pretty clear at this point what’s going on. Feel free to skip ahead, but in an effort to be fair I’ll provide the replies from not one but two HackerOne co-founders (wow a double dungeon release): No change in direction. There is zero training on researcher data. This language isn’t even talking about vulnerability discovery. What happens when you point a “recon agent” at an attack surface? Noise. That’s the context being talked about here – Scope. Out of scope. Informative. Ineligible findings. This same contextual feedback loop is available to researchers (and, increasingly, their agents) through our intake agents & full triage process. We continue to need to do much better on accompanying simplified marketing language with technical architecture documentation, and we need to do a better job at reinforcing the defense in depth narrative – there are no silver bullets here. Nowhere in our vision is a 100% AI human-free future. - Alex Rice and Sorry for the confusion this paragraph has caused. It was meant to capture how our recon agents find out where to focus and where not to focus based on prior results in a customer’s program (mapping the attack surface), not find new vulnerabilities based on researcher submissions. We have adjusted the paragraph in the H1 Continuous Testing page and buttoned up our documentation. H1 Continuous Testing is based on the same approach and methodologies as the H1 Agentic Pentest offering announced in January. Here is the documentation on how those agentic products reason & use context for security testing workflows. But let’s focus on the underlying concern: is H1 using researcher submissions to then deploy agents and find that vulnerability using their techniques in other customers? No. That is a model that can be a win-win-win for everyone in the long run, but we don’t yet have the foundations in place to provide proper recognition and rewards for researchers in such a model. We’re envisioning a platform where researchers drive the frontier, agents provide the scale, and researchers get proper recognition for their impact. Imagine this: you discover a novel technique to find a vulnerability. We operationalize it across every customer’s attack surface that shows signs of exposure. Customers get protected. You get compensated not just for one report, but proportionally to the impact you generate across the platform. That is fundamentally a better deal for researchers than the current one-bounty-per-report model. And it is also a win for customers as it narrows the exposure window. But the reality is that it’s just a vision right now. We are not there yet. This requires careful work across product, policy and researcher engagement models to build it right. Right now, we are still focused on building foundational agentic capabilities for testing, accelerating validation and triage, prioritization, and remediation. These have to work reliably first before we can layer on a researcher-driven attack library and incentive model that does justice to the contribution. We also owe it to customers not to just dump findings on them without the tooling to act on them. The long term is about partnership, not replacement. We want to build incentive structures that support this vision. It’s unexplored territory, and we want to get it right with you. - Michiel Prins along with a HackerOne official™ tweet to calm the masses: Conclusion # Today as I look at HackerOne, it’s hard to even recognize the company that was started back in 2012. The values have shifted, the soul has been gutted, and the core identity has been lost. A sad ending for our hero’s journey. So, where do we go from here? Well, I have some final thoughts for each party involved in this twisting tale. To HackerOne: It was nice knowing you. All I can hope is that you can find your true identity again one day. Although I doubt that will ever happen. To the founders: I hope you got paid well, that you can exit, and that you go do something cool again. To the hackers: Know your worth. Bug bounty platforms cannot exist without hackers. To the companies: You don’t need HackerOne anymore. The tokens to build your own in-house platform cost less than single year of HackerOne. And to whoever is fired up: The market is ready for a disruption. The tools are in your hands. Build what HackerOne could have been. Godspeed and thanks for reading if you made it this far.

sentences.en: They created a HackerOne Community space to organize meetups, online events, workshops, and CTFs.
sentences.zh: 他们创建了一个 HackerOne 社区空间来组织聚会、在线活动、研讨会和 CTF。

sentences.en: They created regional clubs, and appointed hackers who lived there as ambassadors to help foster and grow local researcher communities all around the world.
sentences.zh: 他们创建了地区俱乐部，并任命居住在那里的黑客作为大使，帮助培育和发展世界各地的当地研究人员社区。

blocks.html_en: But slowly but surely, things began to change. The community groups and events lost momentum and fizzled out. The custom designed silkscreen LHE posters became cheap low-effort laser prints. The people who had dedicated years to creating and running incredible events were laid off or left. The LHE invitation and scoring systems became (even more) exclusive, gamified, and exceedingly calculated.

sentences.en: But slowly but surely, things began to change.
sentences.zh: 但慢慢地，但可以肯定的是，事情开始发生变化。

sentences.en: The community groups and events lost momentum and fizzled out.
sentences.zh: 社区团体和活动失去了动力并以失败告终。

sentences.en: The custom designed silkscreen LHE posters became cheap low-effort laser prints.
sentences.zh: 定制设计的丝网印刷 LHE 海报变成了廉价、省力的激光印刷品。

sentences.en: The people who had dedicated years to creating and running incredible events were laid off or left.
sentences.zh: 那些多年来致力于创建和运营令人难以置信的活动的人们被解雇或离开。

sentences.en: The LHE invitation and scoring systems became (even more) exclusive, gamified, and exceedingly calculated.
sentences.zh: LHE 邀请和评分系统变得（甚至更加）排他性、游戏化且经过精心计算。

blocks.html_en: So one by one, the dominoes began to fall.

sentences.en: So one by one, the dominoes began to fall.
sentences.zh: 于是，多米诺骨牌开始一张一张倒下。

blocks.html_en: The Profit Problem #

sentences.en: The Profit Problem #
sentences.zh: 利润问题#

blocks.html_en: Before going further, I think it’s important to get into the “why” behind these changes that started happening. Sometime around 2020 or 2021, HackerOne was forced to come face-to-face with a very important question that every business must ask itself at some point: “How do we make money?”

sentences.en: Before going further, I think it’s important to get into the “why” behind these changes that started happening.
sentences.zh: 在进一步讨论之前，我认为重要的是要了解这些变化开始发生背后的“原因”。

sentences.en: Sometime around 2020 or 2021, HackerOne was forced to come face-to-face with a very important question that every business must ask itself at some point: “How do we make money?”
sentences.zh: 在 2020 年或 2021 年左右的某个时候，HackerOne 被迫面对一个非常重要的问题，每个企业在某个时候都必须问自己：“我们如何赚钱？”

blocks.html_en: To understand how HackerOne even was able to survive as a business, you have to first know that HackerOne was basically running entirely on VC money for the first 10 years of its existence. Between 2014 and 2022, the company did a seed round almost every 2 years, raising a total of $160M. If a company is self-sustaining, there is little-to-no reason to continue raising money unless you have an incredibly high burn-rate, which would be odd for a company with such little infrastructure and technical innovation.

sentences.en: To understand how HackerOne even was able to survive as a business, you have to first know that HackerOne was basically running entirely on VC money for the first 10 years of its existence.
sentences.zh: 要了解 HackerOne 是如何作为一家企业生存下来的，您必须首先知道 HackerOne 在其成立的前 10 年基本上完全依靠风险投资资金运营。

sentences.en: Between 2014 and 2022, the company did a seed round almost every 2 years, raising a total of $160M.
sentences.zh: 2014 年至 2022 年间，该公司几乎每两年进行一次种子轮融资，总共筹集了 1.6 亿美元。

sentences.en: If a company is self-sustaining, there is little-to-no reason to continue raising money unless you have an incredibly high burn-rate, which would be odd for a company with such little infrastructure and technical innovation.
sentences.zh: 如果一家公司是自给自足的，那么除非你的烧钱率非常高，否则几乎没有理由继续筹集资金，这对于一家基础设施和技术创新如此之少的公司来说是很奇怪的。

blocks.html_en: If you know anything about VC, you know how this tends to work; they give you money, and in return, you give them indirect control of the business through board seats, advisory positions, and other leverage mechanisms. The VCs gave the money, so the VCs get the power.

sentences.en: If you know anything about VC, you know how this tends to work; they give you money, and in return, you give them indirect control of the business through board seats, advisory positions, and other leverage mechanisms.
sentences.zh: 如果你对风险投资有所了解，你就会知道它是如何运作的；他们给你钱，作为回报，你通过董事会席位、顾问职位和其他杠杆机制给予他们对业务的间接控制权。

sentences.en: The VCs gave the money, so the VCs get the power.
sentences.zh: 风险投资家给了钱，所以风险投资家获得了权力。

blocks.html_en: Rome did not fall in a day, and neither did HackerOne. The paradigm shift started slowly, and then all at once. The core technology driving the platform began to stagnate. Very little changed within the platform. The UI remained tired and “functional”. The performance remained lacking.

sentences.en: Rome did not fall in a day, and neither did HackerOne.
sentences.zh: 罗马非一日之功，HackerOne 亦非一日之功。

sentences.en: The paradigm shift started slowly, and then all at once.
sentences.zh: 范式转变缓慢地开始，然后突然发生。

sentences.en: The core technology driving the platform began to stagnate.
sentences.zh: 驱动平台的核心技术开始停滞。

sentences.en: Very little changed within the platform.
sentences.zh: 平台内变化很小。

sentences.en: The UI remained tired and “functional”.
sentences.zh: 用户界面仍然陈旧且“功能齐全”。

sentences.en: The performance remained lacking.
sentences.zh: 表现依然欠缺。

blocks.html_en: But the VCs looked at their playbook and realized that the easiest way to make money was simple: get more customers.

sentences.en: But the VCs looked at their playbook and realized that the easiest way to make money was simple: get more customers.
sentences.zh: 但风投们看了他们的剧本，意识到赚钱最简单的方法很简单：获得更多客户。

blocks.html_en: First, the founding CEO was replaced with a corporate CEO. Instead of a 20% cut of bounties paid, they shifted to capacity-based fee structures, annual contracts, and locking customers into multi-year deals.

sentences.en: First, the founding CEO was replaced with a corporate CEO.
sentences.zh: 首先，创始首席执行官被公司首席执行官取代。

sentences.en: Instead of a 20% cut of bounties paid, they shifted to capacity-based fee structures, annual contracts, and locking customers into multi-year deals.
sentences.zh: 他们没有削减 20% 的奖金，而是转向基于容量的收费结构、年度合同，并将客户锁定在多年期交易中。

blocks.html_en: And then, sales. SALES SALES SALES!! They were fully convinced that sales were the bread and butter of the business. So instead of basing the company around hackers, they leaned into sales.

sentences.en: And then, sales.
sentences.zh: 然后是销售。

sentences.en: SALES SALES SALES!!
sentences.zh: 销售销售销售！！

sentences.en: They were fully convinced that sales were the bread and butter of the business.
sentences.zh: 他们完全相信销售是企业的支柱。

sentences.en: So instead of basing the company around hackers, they leaned into sales.
sentences.zh: 因此，他们的公司不再以黑客为基础，而是转向销售。

blocks.html_en: More customers = more annual contracts = more predictable long-term revenue. Once a customer is locked in, they are fed stats and numbers and greased up to keep them happy, but also to keep demands low. When contract renewal comes up, they are given massive (30-60%) discounts in exchange for a multi-year contract in order to keep them locked in and paying.

sentences.en: More customers = more annual contracts = more predictable long-term revenue.
sentences.zh: 更多客户=更多年度合同=更可预测的长期收入。

sentences.en: Once a customer is locked in, they are fed stats and numbers and greased up to keep them happy, but also to keep demands low.
sentences.zh: 一旦锁定了客户，他们就会收到统计数据和数字，并做好准备，让他们满意，同时也保持较低的需求。

sentences.en: When contract renewal comes up, they are given massive (30-60%) discounts in exchange for a multi-year contract in order to keep them locked in and paying.
sentences.zh: 当合同续签时，他们会获得大量（30-60%）折扣，以换取多年合同，以保持他们的锁定并付款。

blocks.html_en: Account Managers would have regular meetings with customers and encourage them to raise bounties to stay competitive and attractive to hackers. They would tell you, “Hackers want to spend time focused on the highest-paying programs”.

sentences.en: Account Managers would have regular meetings with customers and encourage them to raise bounties to stay competitive and attractive to hackers.
sentences.zh: 客户经理将定期与客户会面，鼓励他们提高奖金，以保持竞争力和对黑客的吸引力。

sentences.en: They would tell you, “Hackers want to spend time focused on the highest-paying programs”.
sentences.zh: 他们会告诉你，“黑客希望把时间花在报酬最高的项目上”。

blocks.html_en: HackerOne was proud of this and encouraged the behavior internally. They gave out rewards, free vacations, and encouraged their rapidly growing sales team to sign new customers as much as possible.

sentences.en: HackerOne was proud of this and encouraged the behavior internally.
sentences.zh: HackerOne 对此感到自豪，并在内部鼓励这种行为。

sentences.en: They gave out rewards, free vacations, and encouraged their rapidly growing sales team to sign new customers as much as possible.
sentences.zh: 他们提供奖励、免费假期，并鼓励快速增长的销售团队尽可能多地签约新客户。

blocks.html_en: As this continued, things continued to degrade for everyone involved.

sentences.en: As this continued, things continued to degrade for everyone involved.
sentences.zh: 随着这种情况的继续，每个参与者的情况都在继续恶化。

blocks.html_en: For triagers, the best ones (who were hackers themselves) burned out and quit. The pay was too low and the workload was too much.

sentences.en: For triagers, the best ones (who were hackers themselves) burned out and quit.
sentences.zh: 对于分类者来说，最好的人（他们自己就是黑客）精疲力尽并退出。

sentences.en: The pay was too low and the workload was too much.
sentences.zh: 工资太低，工作量又太大。

blocks.html_en: For hackers, the triage experience declined, and they became flooded with excessive amounts of low-quality programs.

sentences.en: For hackers, the triage experience declined, and they became flooded with excessive amounts of low-quality programs.
sentences.zh: 对于黑客来说，分类体验下降，他们被大量的低质量程序淹没。

blocks.html_en: For customers, the quality of reports went down, the costs went up, and the race to the bottom began.

sentences.en: For customers, the quality of reports went down, the costs went up, and the race to the bottom began.
sentences.zh: 对于客户来说，报告的质量下降了，成本上升了，逐底竞争开始了。

blocks.html_en: And for everyone, the platform experience declined and never evolved.

sentences.en: And for everyone, the platform experience declined and never evolved.
sentences.zh: 对于每个人来说，平台体验都在下降并且从未得到改善。

blocks.html_en: Typically at this point, market economics would dictate that this is where a competitor takes your business and you must improve to retain market share. But bug bounty is an oligopoly, and there are 3 companies that control almost the entire market.

sentences.en: Typically at this point, market economics would dictate that this is where a competitor takes your business and you must improve to retain market share.
sentences.zh: 通常在这一点上，市场经济学会决定这就是竞争对手抢走你的业务的地方，你必须改进以保持市场份额。

sentences.en: But bug bounty is an oligopoly, and there are 3 companies that control almost the entire market.
sentences.zh: 但bug赏金是寡头垄断，有3家公司几乎控制了整个市场。

blocks.html_en: So instead, HackerOne was forced to create a new exclusive opportunity called the “Hacker Success Program” (HSP). This is a dedicated space for top hackers to get direct support from HackerOne for anything bug bounty related. They were assigned to a Hacker Success Manager (HSM) who was employed by HackerOne, and they could leverage that relationship to navigate miscommunications, bad program experiences, low or inaccurate bounty payouts, and much more. They also use this space to offer unique opportunities like H1 challenges for hackers in the HSP group.

sentences.en: So instead, HackerOne was forced to create a new exclusive opportunity called the “Hacker Success Program” (HSP).
sentences.zh: 因此，HackerOne 被迫创建一个新的独家机会，称为“黑客成功计划”(HSP)。

sentences.en: This is a dedicated space for top hackers to get direct support from HackerOne for anything bug bounty related.
sentences.zh: 这是顶级黑客的专用空间，可以从 HackerOne 获得任何与错误赏金相关的直接支持。

sentences.en: They were assigned to a Hacker Success Manager (HSM) who was employed by HackerOne, and they could leverage that relationship to navigate miscommunications, bad program experiences, low or inaccurate bounty payouts, and much more.
sentences.zh: 他们被分配给 HackerOne 雇用的黑客成功经理 (HSM)，他们可以利用这种关系来解决沟通不畅、糟糕的项目体验、低额或不准确的赏金支付等问题。

sentences.en: They also use this space to offer unique opportunities like H1 challenges for hackers in the HSP group.
sentences.zh: 他们还利用这个空间为 HSP 小组中的黑客提供独特的机会，例如 H1 挑战。

blocks.html_en: One thing I want to call out is that while this is a great idea in theory, in practice it created a completely lopsided playing field for new hackers. You have basically zero ways to advocate or work through problems (good luck working with HackerOne support), so the rich get richer and you are given the option to deal with it or get lost unless/until you are a top hacker. Oddly enough, it would be much easier to become a top hacker if you had access to these resources in the first place.

sentences.en: One thing I want to call out is that while this is a great idea in theory, in practice it created a completely lopsided playing field for new hackers.
sentences.zh: 我想指出的一件事是，虽然这在理论上是一个好主意，但在实践中它为新黑客创造了一个完全不平衡的竞争环境。

sentences.en: You have basically zero ways to advocate or work through problems (good luck working with HackerOne support), so the rich get richer and you are given the option to deal with it or get lost unless/until you are a top hacker.
sentences.zh: 你基本上有零种方法来倡导或解决问题（祝你好运，与 HackerOne 支持一起工作），所以富人变得更富，你可以选择处理它或迷失方向，除非/直到你成为顶级黑客。

sentences.en: Oddly enough, it would be much easier to become a top hacker if you had access to these resources in the first place.
sentences.zh: 奇怪的是，如果您首先能够访问这些资源，那么成为顶级黑客就会容易得多。

blocks.html_en: Anyway, for some hackers, the HSP revolutionized what was previously an impossible brick wall. If you got screwed over by a company who failed to understand the security impact of your report, you could now lean on your HSM to help get a direct line of communication to the company and try to resolve that.

sentences.en: Anyway, for some hackers, the HSP revolutionized what was previously an impossible brick wall.
sentences.zh: 不管怎样，对于一些黑客来说，HSP 彻底改变了以前不可能的砖墙。

sentences.en: If you got screwed over by a company who failed to understand the security impact of your report, you could now lean on your HSM to help get a direct line of communication to the company and try to resolve that.
sentences.zh: 如果您被一家无法理解您报告的安全影响的公司搞砸了，您现在可以依靠 HSM 来帮助与该公司建立直接沟通渠道并尝试解决该问题。

blocks.html_en: But for others, the HSP highlighted one of the core underlying failures that has plagued HackerOne for years: stagnating feature development. Even if you are part of the exclusive HSP group, you still don’t have the ability to do one important thing, which is to invoke change and development within the platform.

sentences.en: But for others, the HSP highlighted one of the core underlying failures that has plagued HackerOne for years: stagnating feature development.
sentences.zh: 但对于其他人来说，HSP 强调了多年来困扰 HackerOne 的核心潜在失败之一：功能开发停滞。

sentences.en: Even if you are part of the exclusive HSP group, you still don’t have the ability to do one important thing, which is to invoke change and development within the platform.
sentences.zh: 即使您是专属 HSP 团队的一员，您仍然没有能力做一件重要的事情，即在平台内调用变革和开发。

blocks.html_en: And yet, for some reason, HackerOne decided to take a performative approach to this, going as far as to create a dedicated platform feedback channel, but doing absolutely nothing with any of that feedback. I cannot even count how many pieces of individual feedback and suggestions have been posted in there, with positively zero action from HackerOne.

sentences.en: And yet, for some reason, HackerOne decided to take a performative approach to this, going as far as to create a dedicated platform feedback channel, but doing absolutely nothing with any of that feedback.
sentences.zh: 然而，出于某种原因，HackerOne 决定采取一种执行性的方法来解决这个问题，甚至创建了一个专用的平台反馈渠道，但对任何反馈都没有采取任何行动。

sentences.en: I cannot even count how many pieces of individual feedback and suggestions have been posted in there, with positively zero action from HackerOne.
sentences.zh: 我什至无法计算其中发布了多少条个人反馈和建议，而 HackerOne 的行动积极为零。

blocks.html_en: The AI Era #

sentences.en: The AI Era #
sentences.zh: AI时代#

blocks.html_en: And then, around 2021, we all entered a new period of human history: the rise of AI and LLMs.

sentences.en: And then, around 2021, we all entered a new period of human history: the rise of AI and LLMs.
sentences.zh: 然后，在 2021 年左右，我们都进入了人类历史的一个新时期：人工智能和法学硕士的兴起。

blocks.html_en: Beginning around this time, we all began to witness the huge gains in velocity and the capabilities of LLMs. You could now one-shot features in a fraction of the time, build custom tools, and overall get more done in less time.

sentences.en: Beginning around this time, we all began to witness the huge gains in velocity and the capabilities of LLMs.
sentences.zh: 从这个时候开始，我们都开始见证法学硕士在速度和能力方面的巨大进步。

sentences.en: You could now one-shot features in a fraction of the time, build custom tools, and overall get more done in less time.
sentences.zh: 现在，您可以在很短的时间内完成一次性功能，构建自定义工具，并在更短的时间内完成更多的工作。

blocks.html_en: But this is where HackerOne took a confusing turn. It is truly baffling to me how HackerOne managed to fumble this technology in the worst way possible. They had a 10-year backlog of feature requests, and were handed one of the most powerful software development tools in the last 50 years. But instead of using this to improve the platform and add long-requested features, they decided to move toward creating “their own” AI assistant called Hai. Not only was Hai just a wrapper on top of OpenAI, but it barely had any real unique capabilities to help hackers or programs do what they had been requesting from HackerOne to add to the core platform.

sentences.en: But this is where HackerOne took a confusing turn.
sentences.zh: 但这正是 HackerOne 出现令人困惑的地方。

sentences.en: It is truly baffling to me how HackerOne managed to fumble this technology in the worst way possible.
sentences.zh: 让我真正感到困惑的是，HackerOne 是如何以最糟糕的方式摸索这项技术的。

sentences.en: They had a 10-year backlog of feature requests, and were handed one of the most powerful software development tools in the last 50 years.
sentences.zh: 他们积压了 10 年的功能请求，并获得了过去 50 年来最强大的软件开发工具之一。

sentences.en: But instead of using this to improve the platform and add long-requested features, they decided to move toward creating “their own” AI assistant called Hai.
sentences.zh: 但他们没有用它来改进平台并添加长期要求的功能，而是决定创建“自己的”人工智能助手 Hai。

sentences.en: Not only was Hai just a wrapper on top of OpenAI, but it barely had any real unique capabilities to help hackers or programs do what they had been requesting from HackerOne to add to the core platform.
sentences.zh: Hai 不仅只是 OpenAI 之上的一个包装，而且几乎没有任何真正独特的功能来帮助黑客或程序完成他们要求 HackerOne 添加到核心平台的操作。

blocks.html_en: On top of this, the driving force behind the company, the hackers and co-founders who started the business, were quietly shoved away into the dungeon of HackerOne. The website has them listed as part of the executive team, but they are puppets in their own business, barely getting to work on the product they built from the ground up.

sentences.en: On top of this, the driving force behind the company, the hackers and co-founders who started the business, were quietly shoved away into the dungeon of HackerOne.
sentences.zh: 除此之外，公司背后的推动力，即创办这家公司的黑客和联合创始人，也被悄悄地推入了 HackerOne 的地牢。

sentences.en: The website has them listed as part of the executive team, but they are puppets in their own business, barely getting to work on the product they built from the ground up.
sentences.zh: 该网站将他们列为执行团队的一部分，但他们是自己企业的傀儡，几乎没有开始开发他们从头开始构建的产品。

blocks.html_en: The Enshittification of HackerOne #

sentences.en: The Enshittification of HackerOne #
sentences.zh: HackerOne 的实体化#

blocks.html_en: For almost 10 years, Marten Mickos served as CEO of HackerOne. Some hackers loved Marten; others had mixed feelings. Personally, my interactions with him were somewhere between fine and good. But I do believe that he was very passionate about bug bounty and did a lot of good for the company during his time as CEO.

sentences.en: For almost 10 years, Marten Mickos served as CEO of HackerOne.
sentences.zh: Marten Mickos 担任 HackerOne 首席执行官近 10 年。

sentences.en: Some hackers loved Marten; others had mixed feelings.
sentences.zh: 有些黑客喜欢 Marten；有些黑客则喜欢 Marten。其他人心情复杂。

sentences.en: Personally, my interactions with him were somewhere between fine and good.
sentences.zh: 就我个人而言，我和他的互动介于良好和良好之间。

sentences.en: But I do believe that he was very passionate about bug bounty and did a lot of good for the company during his time as CEO.
sentences.zh: 但我确实相信他对错误赏金非常热衷，并在担任首席执行官期间为公司做了很多好事。

blocks.html_en: But in late 2024, Marten was replaced by Kara Sprague, the former Chief Product Officer at F5. You might be asking yourself, what does a CPO of a networking company know about hacking and bug bounty?

sentences.en: But in late 2024, Marten was replaced by Kara Sprague, the former Chief Product Officer at F5.
sentences.zh: 但在 2024 年底，Marten 被 F5 前首席产品官 Kara Sprague 取代。

sentences.en: You might be asking yourself, what does a CPO of a networking company know about hacking and bug bounty?
sentences.zh: 您可能会问自己，网络公司的 CPO 对黑客攻击和错误赏金了解多少？

blocks.html_en: Honestly, I am not sure. What I will say is that there are mixed signals online regarding what happened to BIG-IP during her time as CPO at F5.

sentences.en: Honestly, I am not sure.

Sorry for the confusion this paragraph has caused. It was meant to capture how our recon agents find out where to focus and where not to focus based on prior results in a customer’s program (mapping the attack surface), not find new vulnerabilities based on researcher submissions. We have adjusted the paragraph in the H1 Continuous Testing page and buttoned up our documentation. H1 Continuous Testing is based on the same approach and methodologies as the H1 Agentic Pentest offering announced in January. Here is the documentation on how those agentic products reason & use context for security testing workflows.

But let’s focus on the underlying concern: is H1 using researcher submissions to then deploy agents and find that vulnerability using their techniques in other customers? No.

That is a model that can be a win-win-win for everyone in the long run, but we don’t yet have the foundations in place to provide proper recognition and rewards for researchers in such a model. We’re envisioning a platform where researchers drive the frontier, agents provide the scale, and researchers get proper recognition for their impact. Imagine this: you discover a novel technique to find a vulnerability. We operationalize it across every customer’s attack surface that shows signs of exposure. Customers get protected. You get compensated not just for one report, but proportionally to the impact you generate across the platform. That is fundamentally a better deal for researchers than the current one-bounty-per-report model. And it is also a win for customers as it narrows the exposure window.

But the reality is that it’s just a vision right now. We are not there yet. This requires careful work across product, policy and researcher engagement models to build it right. Right now, we are still focused on building foundational agentic capabilities for testing, accelerating validation and triage, prioritization, and remediation. These have to work reliably first before we can layer on a researcher-driven attack library and incentive model that does justice to the contribution. We also owe it to customers not to just dump findings on them without the tooling to act on them.

The long term is about partnership, not replacement. We want to build incentive structures that support this vision. It’s unexplored territory, and we want to get it right with you.

content_html_zh:
那么……HackerOne 最近发生了什么？ 可能是时候进行健康检查了。

如果您是 bug 赏金领域的新手（1-3 年），您可能不知道我在说什么。

但作为一个经历过 HackerOne 黄金时代的彻底失败的 bug 赏金猎人，我认为是时候解决房间里的大象了。

就某些背景而言，我于 2017 年开始在 HackerOne 担任黑客。 当我开始从事技术工作时，这种实践经验对于管理错误赏金计划非常有用，因为我知道研究人员想要什么，以及如何与他们互动。

因此，从 2018 年到 2025 年，我在不同公司的 HackerOne 上管理了多个大型错误赏金计划，并且我一直处于等式的两边。

我将要谈论的内容来自作为研究人员和错误赏金项目经理的第一手经验，以及与 HackerOne 多年的公开和私下直接对话。

背景 ＃

首先，我认为了解 HackerOne 的最初设计目的很重要。

2011 年，两位道德黑客 Jobert Abma 和 Michiel Prins 着手寻找 100 家最大科技公司的安全漏洞。 他们成功了，并在 Google、Facebook、Apple、Microsoft、Twitter 和许多其他公司中发现了错误。 此时此刻，道德安全研究的前景充满风险，法律上存疑，并且对安全研究人员来说非常可怕。

不仅个人要承担重大责任，而且在此之前，已经有多起黑客因发现和报告安全漏洞而被刑事指控并被判入狱的事件。 这很大程度上是由于沙子上​​画的特定的任意线造成的，如果交叉，你就会成为一个坏演员，但如果不交叉，你就会成为一个潜在的坏演员，但从技术上讲，这不是一个坏演员。

像 HackerOne 这样的 Bug 赏金平台就是为了直接解决这个问题而设计的。 它为公司和黑客建立了一个安全的相互联系空间，并为道德黑客在获得完全同意的情况下向公司提交安全漏洞并获得报酬铺平了道路。 这是一个巨大的里程碑。 您不必再担心因发现泄露客户数据的 IDOR 而被拖上法庭（或监狱）。 相反，你会得到一句“谢谢”和现金奖励，让每个人都更加安全。

这种运营模式是错误赏金的基础，并在接下来的 5 年多的时间里一直如此。

HackerOne 的黄金时代和现场黑客活动 #

在此期间，业务有一个非常强烈和明确的焦点：我们如何使其成为黑客的最佳产品？

日常经营业务的人是黑客，与黑客相邻，而且大多数（如果不是全部）都定期与黑客面对面。

从 2017 年到 2020 年，HackerOne 每隔几个月就会举办一次现场黑客活动 (LHE)。 这些都是独家活动，世界各地的顶级漏洞赏金研究人员将飞到一个地点，指定一个目标，然后全力寻找关键漏洞。 LHE 是项目的巨大价值支柱。 在 1-3 天的时间内，您将收到比全年收到的更多的高级和关键安全报告。

每场活动都有一张定制设计的海报，上面有图形、黑客用户名、贴纸和挑战币。 对于 HackerOne 及其顶级项目来说，这是一个多么令人难以置信和富有成效的时期，怎么形容都不为过。

这些活动都是独家且备受追捧的。邀请和+1 实际上是他们自己的货币。 这些活动的环境是超现实的。 你将获得世界各地的免费航班和酒店，并与世界上最优秀、最熟练的漏洞赏金猎人一起度过几天。 这些研究人员会定期使用自己的新颖技术发现一些最具影响力的错误，同时在一次性对话中分享无法在其他任何地方复制的提示和技巧。

在现场黑客活动出现之前，大多数安全研究人员的圈子都很小、孤立，公开共享信息几乎是闻所未闻的。 LHE 为安全研究人员创造了一种相互联系的方式，并且本质上在信息安全内创建了一个全新的社区。 现在我最亲密的朋友大多数都是通过现场黑客场景认识的，为此我非常感谢 HackerOne。

LHE 并不是 HackerOne 为安全研究人员构建和建立社区的唯一领域。 他们创建了一个 HackerOne 社区空间来组织聚会、在线活动、研讨会和 CTF。 他们创建了地区俱乐部，并任命居住在那里的黑客作为大使，帮助培育和发展世界各地的当地研究人员社区。

但慢慢地，但可以肯定的是，事情开始发生变化。 社区团体和活动失去了动力并以失败告终。 定制设计的丝网印刷 LHE 海报变成了廉价、省力的激光印刷品。 那些多年来致力于创建和运营令人难以置信的活动的人们被解雇或离开。 LHE 邀请和评分系统变得（甚至更加）排他性、游戏化且经过精心计算。

于是，多米诺骨牌开始一张一张倒下。

利润问题#

在进一步讨论之前，我认为重要的是要了解这些变化开始发生背后的“原因”。 在 2020 年或 2021 年左右的某个时候，HackerOne 被迫面对一个非常重要的问题，每个企业在某个时候都必须问自己：“我们如何赚钱？”

要了解 HackerOne 是如何作为一家企业生存下来的，您必须首先知道 HackerOne 在其成立的前 10 年基本上完全依靠风险投资资金运营。 2014 年至 2022 年间，该公司几乎每两年进行一次种子轮融资，总共筹集了 1.6 亿美元。 如果一家公司是自给自足的，那么除非你的烧钱率非常高，否则几乎没有理由继续筹集资金，这对于一家基础设施和技术创新如此之少的公司来说是很奇怪的。

如果你对风险投资有所了解，你就会知道它是如何运作的；他们给你钱，作为回报，你通过董事会席位、顾问职位和其他杠杆机制给予他们对业务的间接控制权。 风险投资家给了钱，所以风险投资家获得了权力。

罗马非一日之功，HackerOne 亦非一日之功。 范式转变缓慢地开始，然后突然发生。 驱动平台的核心技术开始停滞。 平台内变化很小。 用户界面仍然陈旧且“功能齐全”。 表现依然欠缺。

但风投们看了他们的剧本，意识到赚钱最简单的方法很简单：获得更多客户。

首先，创始首席执行官被公司首席执行官取代。 他们没有削减 20% 的奖金，而是转向基于容量的收费结构、年度合同，并将客户锁定在多年期交易中。

然后是销售。 销售销售销售！！ 他们完全相信销售是企业的支柱。 因此，他们的公司不再以黑客为基础，而是转向销售。

更多客户=更多年度合同=更可预测的长期收入。 一旦锁定了客户，他们就会收到统计数据和数字，并做好准备，让他们满意，同时也保持较低的需求。 当合同续签时，他们会获得大量（30-60%）折扣，以换取多年合同，以保持他们的锁定并付款。

客户经理将定期与客户会面，鼓励他们提高奖金，以保持竞争力和对黑客的吸引力。 他们会告诉你，“黑客希望把时间花在报酬最高的项目上”。

HackerOne 对此感到自豪，并在内部鼓励这种行为。 他们提供奖励、免费假期，并鼓励快速增长的销售团队尽可能多地签约新客户。

随着这种情况的继续，每个参与者的情况都在继续恶化。

对于分类者来说，最好的人（他们自己就是黑客）精疲力尽并退出。 工资太低，工作量又太大。

对于黑客来说，分类体验下降，他们被大量的低质量程序淹没。

对于客户来说，报告的质量下降了，成本上升了，逐底竞争开始了。

对于每个人来说，平台体验都在下降并且从未得到改善。

通常在这一点上，市场经济学会决定这就是竞争对手抢走你的业务的地方，你必须改进以保持市场份额。 但bug赏金是寡头垄断，有3家公司几乎控制了整个市场。

因此，HackerOne 被迫创建一个新的独家机会，称为“黑客成功计划”(HSP)。 这是顶级黑客的专用空间，可以从 HackerOne 获得任何与错误赏金相关的直接支持。 他们被分配给 HackerOne 雇用的黑客成功经理 (HSM)，他们可以利用这种关系来解决沟通不畅、糟糕的项目体验、低额或不准确的赏金支付等问题。 他们还利用这个空间为 HSP 小组中的黑客提供独特的机会，例如 H1 挑战。

我想指出的一件事是，虽然这在理论上是一个好主意，但在实践中它为新黑客创造了一个完全不平衡的竞争环境。 你基本上有零种方法来倡导或解决问题（祝你好运，与 HackerOne 支持一起工作），所以富人变得更富，你可以选择处理它或迷失方向，除非/直到你成为顶级黑客。 奇怪的是，如果您首先能够访问这些资源，那么成为顶级黑客就会容易得多。

不管怎样，对于一些黑客来说，HSP 彻底改变了以前不可能的砖墙。 如果您被一家无法理解您报告的安全影响的公司搞砸了，您现在可以依靠 HSM 来帮助与该公司建立直接沟通渠道并尝试解决该问题。

但对于其他人来说，HSP 强调了多年来困扰 HackerOne 的核心潜在失败之一：功能开发停滞。 即使您是专属 HSP 团队的一员，您仍然没有能力做一件重要的事情，即在平台内调用变革和开发。

然而，出于某种原因，HackerOne 决定采取一种执行性的方法来解决这个问题，甚至创建了一个专用的平台反馈渠道，但对任何反馈都没有采取任何行动。 我什至无法计算其中发布了多少条个人反馈和建议，而 HackerOne 的行动积极为零。

AI时代#

然后，在 2021 年左右，我们都进入了人类历史的一个新时期：人工智能和法学硕士的兴起。

从这个时候开始，我们都开始见证法学硕士在速度和能力方面的巨大进步。 现在，您可以在很短的时间内完成一次性功能，构建自定义工具，并在更短的时间内完成更多的工作。

但这正是 HackerOne 出现令人困惑的地方。 让我真正感到困惑的是，HackerOne 是如何以最糟糕的方式摸索这项技术的。 他们积压了 10 年的功能请求，并获得了过去 50 年来最强大的软件开发工具之一。 但他们没有用它来改进平台并添加长期要求的功能，而是决定创建“自己的”人工智能助手 Hai。 Hai 不仅只是 OpenAI 之上的一个包装，而且几乎没有任何真正独特的功能来帮助黑客或程序完成他们要求 HackerOne 添加到核心平台的操作。

除此之外，公司背后的推动力，即创办这家公司的黑客和联合创始人，也被悄悄地推入了 HackerOne 的地牢。 该网站将他们列为执行团队的一部分，但他们是自己企业的傀儡，几乎没有开始开发他们从头开始构建的产品。

HackerOne 的实体化#

Marten Mickos 担任 HackerOne 首席执行官近 10 年。 有些黑客喜欢 Marten；有些黑客则喜欢 Marten。其他人心情复杂。 就我个人而言，我和他的互动介于良好和良好之间。 但我确实相信他对错误赏金非常热衷，并在担任首席执行官期间为公司做了很多好事。

但在 2024 年底，Marten 被 F5 前首席产品官 Kara Sprague 取代。 您可能会问自己，网络公司的 CPO 对黑客攻击和错误赏金了解多少？

老实说，我不确定。 我要说的是，关于 BIG-IP 在 F5 担任 CPO 期间发生的事情，网上有不同的信号。

但这并没有阻止董事会认为她是公司未来的合适人选。 这并不是 HackerOne 做出的一系列可疑商业决策中的第一个，也不是最后一个。

随着AI代理不断成长并转变为各种身份，HackerOne的身份也开始转变。 HackerOne 缓慢而稳定地围绕一个新发明的行业类别重塑了自己的品牌：“CTEM”，即“持续威胁暴露管理”。

HackerOne 很快开始发展成为一家痴迷于数字、业务目标和 B2B 销售的没有灵魂的公司。 他们从谈论错误赏金计划、现场黑客活动以及如何帮助您保持安全，转而宣传他们的内部人工智能安全产品和持续安全监控工具。

等等，什么？ 什么内部人工智能安全产品？

我们保证，您的报告就是您的#

有时，这一切都始于一条推文。

2026 年 2 月，知名黑客 zseano 注意到 HackerOne 员工离职人数激增，并询问为什么会发生这种情况。

这最终表明 HackerOne 已经进行了 ToS 更新，使得在 HackerOne 上提交的报告可以用于训练人工智能模型。

正如您所料，这会产生相当多的噪音，尤其是在 HSP 聊天中。 我注意到的一件事是，现代的 HackerOne 只会让创始人走出地牢来控制损害，而这是拉动杠杆的最佳时机。

24 小时内，Alex Rice，联合创始人、CTO（和 CISO……？） HackerOne 从地牢中出来执行损害控制。 （这是自两年前创建 HSP 一般聊天以来他第一次在该聊天中发消息）。

我们不会在研究人员数据上训练、微调或以其他方式改进 GenAI 或大型语言模型。 其中包括 Agentic PTaaS。 https://docs.hackerone.com/en/articles/10908081-hai-security-trust

当被要求删除 ToS 的第 3.1 节时，Alex 承诺将在即将发布的 ToS 更新中解决这一问题并使其更加明确。

一周之内，首席执行官卡拉·斯普拉格 (Kara Sprague) 就被卷入其中，并在 LinkedIn 上发表了一篇空洞的帖子，解释说

HackerOne 不会在内部或通过第三方提供商根据研究人员提交的材料或客户机密数据来训练生成式 AI 模型。 研究人员提交的内容不会用于训练、微调或以其他方式改进生成式人工智能模型。 这适用于我们的整个平台，包括我们的 Agentic PTaaS 产品和平台内 AI Hai 中使用的功能。

Alex Rice 甚至还参加了 Critical Thinking Bug Bounty 播客，并做了一个客座演讲，专门讨论了这个问题，并消除了对报告数据用于训练 AI 模型的任何担忧。

太神奇了，事情就这样解决了。 HackerOne 不使用研究人员数据来训练人工智能模型。

…Right?

只是开玩笑，他们从来都不是#

对我们来说不幸的是，当今的 HackerOne 遵循了一个相当令人印象深刻的公关损害控制策略：

  1. 解决恐惧
  2. 缓解担忧
  3. 不要改变任何东西

这部戏剧发生大约两个月后，有人在 HSP 聊天中提到，他们注意到黑客代理对他们的一份报告的评论，并想知道这是人工智能代理还是真人。

HackerOne 的一位产品经理的回应是：

这是人工智能所做的初步审查[...] H1 分类过程有一个称为“H1 摄入”的步骤 [...] 我们对某些报告进行了自动化处理，以确保它们更快地到达“验证团队”。

当被问及“某些报告”是否意味着某些报告类型或者程序是否可以在任何地方启用它时，他们回答道：

我们正在对所有报告进行分析，人工智能确定哪些内容可以直接发送给验证团队，哪些内容需要首先由接收团队的人员审核。 […] 该系统还可以从行为中学习，因此，如果建议被拒绝 [...] 委员会在提出建议时也会考虑到这些因素。

等一下。

我认为研究人员提交的内容不用于训练、微调或以其他方式改进生成人工智能模型。

但现在所有报告都通过人工智能系统运行，该系统正在使用这些报告的结果来影响它处理未来报告的方式。 那么这在技术上是“微调”吗？ 从技术上来说，不。

那么这两件事怎么可能呢？

好吧，当我问这个问题时，我收到了亚历克斯·赖斯 (Alex Rice) 在二月份所说的话的令人难以置信的复制粘贴回复：

Hai 不会根据客户或研究人员的数据训练、微调或以其他方式改进 GenAI 或大型语言模型：https://docs.hackerone.com/en/articles/10908081-hai-security-trust

然后他们提出了一个似乎与此相矛盾的解释：

在数据库中存储学习内容与训练/微调模型的行为方式不同。 我们将拒绝原因存储在数据库中，以交叉引用并增强代理在确定后续步骤时所做的推理。 […] 代理将从客户在过去的报告中所做的行为中获取这一点，并用它来记忆和增强新报告的推理。

所以，是的，HackerOne 并不是根据您的报告数据构建模型权重，也不是传统意义上的“训练”。

但对于使用数据的研究人员来说，这种区别并没有任何有意义的区别。 该系统仍在从实际意义上重要的报告数据中学习：过去的报告会改变未来的自动化行为。

你可以称之为记忆、检索、情境学习，或者任何你想要的东西。 为了确定研究人员数据是否用于改进系统，这种区别在功能上是等效的。

更重要的是，几天后，HackerOne 发表了一篇博客文章，指出：

随着人工智能辅助提交的数量不断增加，我们在自己的平台上大力投资人工智能驱动的分类和验证。 我们的代理人工智能系统 Hai 现在与我们的人类安全分析师一起处理传入报告的初始分类、重复数据删除和验证。

沸点#

至此，我对 HackerOne 失去了所有信心。 我已经存在了这么多年，经历了这么多赛季，所以没有必要放弃任何事情。

因此，我在 HSP 聊天中发布了一条很长的消息，呼应了我在本博客中所说的许多内容。

结果发生的事情实际上非常令人惊讶：HSP 中的许多其他顶级黑客都表示同意，回应了同样的担忧，并呼吁进行变革。

我想，HackerOne 肯定必须对此做出回应。

他们做到了。

联合创始人 Michiel Prins 被允许离开 HackerOne 地牢，通过 AI 响应的绝对危险来执行损害控制：

你说这一点是对的。 平台的某些部分和整体体验的发展速度不够快，这令人沮丧。 我们一直优先考虑改善客户和研究人员成果的工作。 分类就是一个明显的例子。 速度和一致性有了实质性的提高，这对平台上的每个人都很重要。 报告助手可能不是针对此渠道中的高水平黑客，但它对于社区的最大部分（职业生涯早期的黑客）来说是一个显着的增强，这导致了更清晰的分类报告，以分析和加速整体吞吐量。 与此同时，人工智能正在发生更大的转变。 关于人工智能取代安全研究人员的声音很多。 我们不相信这一点。 我们正在投资以确保研究人员变得更加重要，而不是变得更加重要。 大部分工作都发生在市场的客户端。 也就是说，您所指出的日常可用性和根据反馈采取行动之间的差距是真实存在的。 我们需要在这方面做得更好，我们需要更清楚地展示这一进展。

然后，按照剧本，他们等待社区继续前进，将其掩盖起来，但什么都没有改变。

直到 6 月份，情况确实如此，当时 rez0（批判性思维错误赏金播客的联合主持人）询问了刚刚推出的新“HackerOne 持续测试”产品：

HackerOne 立即试图反击并声称这实际上不是真的。 我发现很难理解一家公司如何与自己的价值观如此脱节，但只有当它是由仔细观察并提出问题的黑客提出的时候。

过去几个月的所有行为都体现了“哎呀，我们不是故意大声说出安静的部分”，当然不是“我们不这样做”。
